cards.text: Public health information moves continuously and bidirectionally, with evidence and guidance moving outward through trusted community partners and local knowledge flowing back into institutional public health. Community input is part of routine practice rather than periodic.
Core public health functions, resources, and responsibilities are distributed across a broader trusted public health ecosystem that includes institutional public health and community partners

Community relationships are treated as essential infrastructure and receive sustained funding, which allows public health to reach those they previously struggled to reach while creating a new vulnerability: "un-networked" individuals and communities

Trust is placed in people and relationships within networks rather than institutions by default, raising questions around accountability when trust is broken and requiring institutional public health to continually earn and maintain trust and credibility

The divide in this future, and the inequities that result (much like present times), is about who is connected to networks, who can navigate an increasingly noisy environment, and who has the capacity to quickly assess or verify often competing public health information

Surveillance and disease detection are automated, but since information can come from many different networks and moves quickly alongside misinformation, power and influence comes from being able to verify and share information.
Governmental public health agencies have fewer staff
Less formal public health training programs
the public health workforce has less standardized approaches
There is greater attention and respect to learned and lived experience
the rise of grifters pretending to have experience that they don't to monetize information sharing
People give money and resources to bad actors
Communities/people become more desperate for correct information and wealth/knowledge gaps widen
Backlash of younger people against media platforms/leaders/grifters
Creates a population that is difficult to reach over certain mediums by reputable institutions
Surveillance is no longer a core public health function and considered as valuable
Because of the automation, disease detection and surveillance data is not shared
Larger populations drop out of using platforms that use automation
Third sector is created to verify information
Corporate (profit) and political incentives to control verification sectors
Individualized public health reporting based on personalized metrics and location (to monetize)
People are further connected to corporate products and individual data is owned by corps
Remaining agency staff mostly coordinate and support partners

unclustered.text: Needs and disagreements outside those recognized voices become less visible in public health decisions.

unclustered.text: Concern about fabricated experience increases demands for genuine community messengers to prove their identity and experience.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: If proof requires formal records or credentials, people with valuable but undocumented experience lose access to recognized partner roles.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Money lost to deceptive advice leaves affected households with fewer resources to meet health needs or take protective action.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies redirect outreach toward known community intermediaries and in-person contact to reach people withdrawing from distrusted channels.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Reaching people who withdraw from distrusted channels through personal contact takes more staff and partner time.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: If reduced status leads to less human oversight of automated surveillance, responsibility for questioning and investigating suspect outputs becomes unclear.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Where underlying data are withheld, local agencies and partners cannot independently assess how an alert applies to their communities.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Disputes about the evidence take longer to resolve, delaying coordinated action.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies lose contact with people who leave the platforms those agencies rely on for communication.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Verification providers using different methods can reach conflicting judgments about the same alert.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: People turn to verifiers they already trust, so verification can reproduce existing divisions between networks.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: If verification is sold as a premium service, ability to pay shapes how quickly communities can check alerts.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Community organizations pool resources for shared verification, reducing reliance on individual subscriptions.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Changing providers becomes difficult where personal records and verification histories cannot be transferred.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Personalized alerts give people in the same community different pictures of risk, making agreement on collective action harder.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Partners bring their own missions and constituencies, giving the strongest partners disproportionate influence over ecosystem priorities.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Populations without a strong partner receive less attention even when their needs are high.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies retain or rebuild direct capacity to reach populations that no partner represents.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Where agency delivery capacity has been reduced, a partner’s loss of staff, funding, or operating capacity leaves functions without an immediate replacement.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies fund overlapping partner capacity, adding standby and coordination costs.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Partners formalize mutual aid arrangements to share the work and cost of maintaining backup capacity.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: When functions are shared, outcomes are harder to attribute to any one organization.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Funders and elected officials face more uncertainty about organizational performance, changing how they make funding decisions.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Accreditation and performance measures are revised to account for work carried out across the ecosystem.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Correcting a trusted messenger who is sincerely wrong can damage a relationship the agency depends on.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies negotiate corrections privately and ask the messenger to deliver them, which can delay the correction.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Some corrections never reach the people who heard the original claim.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Trusted local figures become valuable impersonation targets, especially where communities have few reliable ways to check a message’s source.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Partners ask agencies for tools and training that help people confirm a message really came from them.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies support partners’ identity verification and trusted communication channels alongside providing evidence.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Members of a trusted network have interests that shape when and whether the network acts, as with the venue owner in the scenario.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: When agencies respond to a partner’s conflicted decisions by withdrawing support, they also risk losing reach into that community.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies use conflict disclosures and agreed response rules to preserve partnerships, but some partners experience these as institutional distrust.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Population signals such as wastewater and school absences gain value when agreement across independent sources makes an event harder to dismiss.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Where budgets are fixed, investment in population-level sensing grows at the expense of individual reporting.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Where signals cover broad areas, communities dispute which neighborhoods or workplaces are affected even when they accept an outbreak is real.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Confirming an alert’s source and whether it has been altered becomes a function in its own right, needing staff, standards, and rapid decisions.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Because false alerts can spread faster than corrections, agencies and partners establish ways to authenticate official messages before a crisis.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Early standard-setters shape which forms of proof count, and vendors or platforms may set rules that public health must follow.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Laboratories and data systems become targets for discrediting as well as for disruption.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Agencies publish methods, uncertainty, and shareable underlying signals to defend their credibility.
unclustered.author: Facilitator

unclustered.text: Critics use disclosed limitations to challenge agencies, so transparency increases both public scrutiny and exposure to selective attacks.
unclustered.author: Facilitator
